responses.title: Home for contemporary African culture and heritage in London
responses.description: Established in 1964, The Africa Centre exists to educate, connect, and advocate for Africa and its global diaspora. We facilitate and lead empowering conversations about Africa, inspired by the vision of our forebears and the fresh consciousness of a new generation of pan-Africanist thinkers and innovators.

  • A Quiet Scream, The Numbers Behind The Africa Centre Crisis - Dr Sheila Obim

    The Africa Centre faces an urgent financial crisis that threatens its Southwark home and future. In this reflection, Trustee Dr Sheila Obim highlights the Centre’s 60-year legacy as a vital cultural home for Africans and the diaspora, calling for transparency, community ownership and collective action. Through the “Our Africa Centre. Our Heritage. Our Future.” campaign and Harambee Circles, supporters are invited to help secure a sustainable future for generations to come. Read more

  • CEO BLOG #31 – WHEN THE LIGHTS WENT OFF IN SOUTHWARK

    The Africa Centre has temporarily closed its doors due to ongoing financial challenges, despite years of recovery efforts. In response, supporters rallied in solidarity, reaffirming the Centre’s vital role as a cultural home for African communities. A fundraising campaign aims to raise £100,000 to reopen the institution and secure a stronger, sustainable future for it. Read more

Our Africa Centre, Our Heritage, Our Future

Our Story

Originally conceived to foster non-governmental relations between newly independent Africa and Britain, The Africa Centre's mission is to educate, connect, and advocate for Africa and its diaspora. Previously located in Covent Garden, London for over five decades, we launched our new HQ in Southwark in June 2022.

Published: 17th March, 2016

Author:

Our Spaces

The Africa Centre is a home from home and offers welcoming and exciting spaces from our restaurant and bar to event spaces featuring live music , exhibitions and Africa Centre programme. You can also hire our spaces for your own event, be it a social occasion, team away day or community event.

Published: 18th March, 2021

Author:

Our Impact

60
 Six decades of championing the cause for Africa and its diaspora. We'll be celebrating our 60th anniversary in 2024.
£100K The total amount of funding from our latest successful application to the Wolfson Foundation.
8000 The number of people who attended our last free summer festival in Southwark, London in 2018.

Opinion

  • CEO BLOG #31 – WHEN THE LIGHTS WENT OFF IN SOUTHWARK

    The Africa Centre has temporarily closed its doors due to ongoing financial challenges, despite years of recovery efforts. In response, supporters rallied in solidarity, reaffirming the Centre’s vital role as a cultural home for African communities. A fundraising campaign aims to raise £100,000 to reopen the institution and secure a stronger, sustainable future for it. Read more

  • CEO BLOG #30 JULY 2026

    As the 2026 World Cup unfolded, I found myself reflecting on something much bigger than football. Across almost every squad, players of African descent were among the tournament's defining figures. Africa is no longer simply a continent; it is a global people. Pan-Africanism began as consciousness, then became liberation, and is now becoming belonging: the Global African at home in many worlds at once. And as Wole Soyinka reminded us, culture must now do the heavy lifting. Read more

  • CEO BLOG #29 JUNE 2026: A LEGACY ACTIVATED

    The Africa Centre wrapped up its 60th-anniversary exhibition after months of extensions and global praise, with content preserved online and archived. Leadership at the Young Africa Centre passed to new co-chairs continuing youth-led programming. Upcoming: a leadership book launch, an RCA exhibition, and a Wole Soyinka cultural programme. The newsletter also reflects on Africa's historic World Cup presence, and debates fan loyalty amid South Africa's anti-immigration tensions. Read more

Wole Soyinka international Cultural exchange 2026 presents Esther’s Revenge

Esther’s Revenge is an immersive, participatory play inspired by true events from 1953. Facing a death-by-hanging sentence, Esther guides audiences through the circumstances leading to Mark’s death, exploring racial discrimination, gender-based violence, sexual abuse, and social injustice. Audience members act as jurors, weighing evidence and ultimately deciding whether Esther’s execution should proceed. Read more

A royal College of Art Africa Society Exhibition - Translation issues

"Translation Issues" explores the meanings, memories and emotions embedded in African languages, gestures and cultural practices that often resist direct translation. Curated by the Royal College of Art Africa Society in collaboration with The Africa Centre, the exhibition examines how diaspora communities navigate cultural transmission across generations, inviting audiences to reflect on the challenge of communicating the untranslatable and preserving cultural memory. Zainab, an expert driller, takes charge of a high-stakes offshore oil rig as the only woman among a hostile, hardened crew.
